title: Long method
description: A method that does not fit on a screen is doing more than one thing: the smell is length, the disease is mixed abstraction levels. Detection is simple — lines over N, or better, cyclomatic complexity over N — but the fix (Extract Method) needs judgment about where the seams are. Long methods correlate strongly with bug density; splitting them is the highest-ROI refactoring there is.
mechanism: Metrics: LOC, cyclomatic complexity, number of local variables. Thresholds (e.g., >30 lines or complexity >10) flag candidates; human confirms the seam. Extract Method with intention-revealing names.
algo: O(methods) metrics. Complexity via branch counting on the AST.
demo:
import ast

src = '''def process(order):
    total = 0
    for i in order.items:
        if i.taxable:
            total += i.price * 1.2
        else:
            total += i.price
    if order.coupon:
        total *= 0.9
    if total > 100:
        total -= 10
    log(total)
    notify(order.user, total)
    return total
'''
tree = ast.parse(src)
fn = tree.body[0]
branches = sum(1 for n in ast.walk(fn) if isinstance(n, (ast.If, ast.For, ast.While)))
loc = fn.end_lineno - fn.lineno
print('process(): %d lines, %d branches' % (loc, branches))
print('smell:', 'LONG METHOD' if loc > 10 or branches > 3 else 'ok',
      '-> Extract Method at the seams (pricing / logging / notify)')

title: God class
description: A god class knows too much and does too much — hundreds of methods, dozens of fields, every feature touching it. Detection: weighted method count, number of fields, and coupling (how many other classes it touches). The fix is Extract Class: group methods by the fields they use (cluster by field access) and split along those lines. God classes are where merge conflicts go to breed.
mechanism: Metrics: WMC (sum of method complexities), ATFD (accesses to foreign data), TCC (tight class cohesion). Low TCC + high WMC = god class. Split by field-usage clustering.
algo: O(classes * methods) metrics; field-usage clustering for the split.
demo:
# TCC (tight class cohesion): fraction of method pairs sharing a field. Low = god class.
import itertools
methods = {  # method -> fields it touches
    'charge': {'balance', 'ledger'}, 'refund': {'balance', 'ledger'},
    'send_email': {'smtp'}, 'render_pdf': {'template'},
}
pairs = list(itertools.combinations(methods, 2))
shared = sum(1 for a, b in pairs if methods[a] & methods[b])
tcc = shared / len(pairs)
print('method pairs sharing fields: %d/%d (TCC=%.2f)' % (shared, len(pairs), tcc))
print('verdict:', 'GOD CLASS: split billing {charge,refund} from comms {send_email,render_pdf}' if tcc < 0.3 else 'cohesive')

title: Duplicated code
description: Duplication is the root smell — every other smell is easier to fix when the code exists once. Detection is the clone-detection database's job (token/AST matching); the smell record here is about policy: duplication budget per PR, the 'rule of three' (tolerate twice, abstract on the third), and distinguishing harmful duplication (logic) from harmless (test fixtures, generated code).
mechanism: Clone detector on the diff; budget: no new clones over N tokens; rule of three for abstraction timing. Exemptions: generated code, tests (sometimes), configuration.
algo: O(diff) incremental. Policy, not just tooling — the budget makes it stick.
demo:
from difflib import SequenceMatcher

a = 'def discount(p): return p * 0.9 if p > 100 else p'
b = 'def discount2(p): return p * 0.9 if p > 100 else p'
c = 'def tax(p): return p * 1.2'

for name, x in (('b (copy)', b), ('c (different)', c)):
    r = SequenceMatcher(None, a, x).ratio()
    print('%-13s similarity %.2f %s' % (name, r, '-> DUPLICATION SMELL' if r > 0.85 else ''))
print('rule of three: seen twice, tolerate; third time, abstract')

title: Feature envy
description: Feature envy is a method that uses another class's data more than its own — it wishes it lived there. Detection: count accesses to foreign fields vs own fields; envy when foreign dominates. The fix is Move Method: relocate the method to the envied class (or Extract Method for the envying part). Envy is how misplaced responsibilities reveal themselves.
mechanism: ATFD (access to foreign data) vs local access per method. Move Method refactoring; update all callers. IDEs automate the move including reference updates.
algo: O(methods * accesses) counting. The move is mechanical; choosing the target is judgment.

title: Shotgun surgery
description: Shotgun surgery is when one logical change requires edits scattered across dozens of files — the knowledge is spread too thin. Detection: co-change analysis from version history (files that always change together) plus change-size metrics. The fix is to consolidate: move the scattered logic behind one interface (often revealing a missing abstraction). Divergent change is its twin: one file changed for many unrelated reasons.
mechanism: Mine co-change sets from VCS history; flag files changed together > threshold. Consolidate via Extract Class / Move Method toward the abstraction the changes imply.
algo: O(commits * files) mining. Co-change coupling is the signal.

title: Metrics thresholds
description: Smell detection needs thresholds — complexity > 10, method > 30 lines, class > 500 lines — and thresholds need calibration, not folklore. The honest method: measure the metric distribution on your codebase, set thresholds at the tail (95th percentile), and ratchet down over time. Universal thresholds misfire; calibrated ones match what your team actually feels as smelly.
mechanism: Compute metric histograms per codebase; set initial thresholds at p95; review flagged items; adjust. Track threshold changes in version control — they are policy.
algo: O(codebase) measurement; thresholds at distribution tails.
demo:
import statistics
# calibrate: threshold at the tail of YOUR distribution, not folklore
complexities = [2, 3, 1, 5, 4, 2, 8, 3, 2, 25, 4, 3, 30, 2, 1, 6, 3, 2, 18]
# p95 threshold
s = sorted(complexities)
p95 = s[int(0.95 * len(s))]
print('complexity p50=%d p95=%d max=%d' % (statistics.median(s), p95, max(s)))
print('calibrated threshold: flag complexity > %d (the tail), not folklore "10"' % p95)
print('ratchet down as the codebase improves; thresholds are policy, versioned')

title: AST rule-based detection
description: Many smells are AST patterns: empty except blocks, mutable default arguments, wildcard imports, deeply nested conditionals. Rule-based detectors encode each as an AST visitor — precise, fast, explainable. The catalog grows with experience; each rule carries its rationale and fix. This is the bread and butter of linters, and it catches what metrics miss (a 5-line method can still be smelly).
mechanism: Visitor per rule over the AST; report with location and message. Rules compose; suppressions are explicit comments. Custom rules encode team conventions.
algo: O(nodes * rules) single pass. Precision high; recall limited to encoded patterns.

title: ML-based smell detection
description: ML smell detectors learn from labeled corpora instead of hand-written rules: features from metrics, tokens, and AST shapes feed classifiers that flag 'smelly' methods. They catch patterns no rule encodes — but they need labeled data (expensive), they are black boxes (why is this flagged?), and they drift as code style evolves. Best used as a triage layer over rule-based detection, not a replacement.
mechanism: Features: metric vectors + embeddings; labels: expert-tagged smells; model: gradient boosting / small nets. Explain via feature importance. Retrain per codebase for calibration.
algo: Training O(labeled * features); inference O(features) per method. Labels are the bottleneck.
demo:
# ML smell detection, honestly: a tiny classifier over metric features
# features: (loc, complexity, params, foreign_accesses)
X = [(45, 12, 6, 9), (8, 2, 2, 1), (60, 15, 8, 12), (10, 3, 1, 0), (50, 4, 7, 2)]
y = [1, 0, 1, 0, 1]  # expert labels: 1 = smelly

def score(feats):  # toy 'model': weighted metrics (real ones learn these weights)
    loc, cx, params, foreign = feats
    return 0.3 * loc + 2.0 * cx + 3.0 * params + 1.5 * foreign

for feats, label in zip(X, y):
    s = score(feats)
    print('features=%-22s score=%5.1f label=%d %s' % (feats, s, label, 'OK' if (s > 40) == label else 'MISS'))
print('real models learn the weights; labels are expensive; use as triage over rules')

title: Severity ranking
description: Not all smells deserve equal attention: severity ranking orders findings by (impact x likelihood x cost-to-fix). A god class in the payment path outranks a long method in a test helper. Ranking inputs: churn (smelly + frequently changed = risky), centrality (many dependents), and bug history. The ranked list is the refactoring backlog — top items first, and the list is short on purpose.
mechanism: score = severity_weight * churn * centrality * bug_correlation. Sort; take the top N as the backlog. Re-rank monthly — the codebase moves.
algo: O(findings) scoring with precomputed churn/centrality. The backlog is the product.
demo:
# rank smells: impact x churn x centrality -> the refactoring backlog
findings = [
    ('god class: payments', 9, 30, 12),
    ('long method: test helper', 4, 2, 1),
    ('feature envy: checkout', 7, 25, 8),
    ('duplication: logging', 3, 40, 20),
]
ranked = sorted(findings, key=lambda f: f[1] * f[2] * f[3], reverse=True)
print('%-26s %6s' % ('smell', 'score'))
for name, sev, churn, central in ranked:
    print('%-26s %6d' % (name, sev * churn * central))
print('top of list = do first; the backlog is short on purpose')

title: Auto-fix suggestions
description: Some smells have mechanical fixes: unused imports (delete), mutable defaults (None + guard), long parameter lists (introduce parameter object — semi-mechanical). Auto-fixers apply the safe ones and suggest the rest as diffs. The safety bar is high — a fixer must never change behavior — so fixes are limited to semantics-preserving transforms with test verification after.
mechanism: Transform catalog: pattern -> rewrite, each proven semantics-preserving. Apply; run affected tests; revert on failure. Suggest (don't apply) the judgment-call fixes.
algo: O(findings) transforms; test verification bounds the risk.
demo:
import ast

# auto-fix: mutable default argument -> None + guard (semantics-preserving)
src = 'def f(xs=[]):\n    return xs\n'
tree = ast.parse(src)

class Fix(ast.NodeTransformer):
    def visit_FunctionDef(self, node):
        for i, d in enumerate(node.args.defaults):
            if isinstance(d, ast.List):
                node.args.defaults[i] = ast.Constant(value=None)
                guard = ast.parse('if %s is None: %s = []' % (
                    node.args.args[-len(node.args.defaults) + i].arg,
                    node.args.args[-len(node.args.defaults) + i].arg)).body[0]
                node.body.insert(0, guard)
        return node

fixed = Fix().visit(tree)
print(ast.unparse(fixed))
print('mechanical, semantics-preserving, test-verified: the auto-fix bar')

title: Divergent change
description: Divergent change is one module changed for many unrelated reasons — the sign it has too many responsibilities. Detection: commit analysis showing the file touched by unrelated features, or simply many distinct reasons in its history. The fix is Extract Class along the change-reasons: each reason becomes its own module. It is shotgun surgery's twin: scattered changes vs scattered reasons.
mechanism: Mine commit messages / ticket links per file; cluster change reasons; >N distinct reasons = divergent. Split along the reason clusters.
algo: O(commits) reason mining. The reasons come from human-written messages — noisy but telling.

title: Data clumps
description: Data clumps are variables that travel together — (x, y), (start, end), (host, port) — appearing as parameter groups across methods. The smell is the missing abstraction: they want to be a class. Detection: find parameter groups co-occurring in multiple signatures. The fix (Introduce Parameter Object) simplifies signatures and gives the concept a name and a home for its behavior.
mechanism: Mine parameter lists; find frequent co-occurring subsets (association mining); suggest the object. Behavior follows: methods using only the clump move to the new class.
algo: O(signatures) frequent-itemset mining on parameter sets.

title: Primitive obsession
description: Primitive obsession is using raw ints and strings for domain concepts — phone numbers as str, money as float. The bugs it breeds are legendary (float money, stringly-typed everything). Detection: parameters of the same primitive type in confusing orders, validation scattered everywhere. The fix is tiny value classes (PhoneNumber, Money) with validation in one place — the cheapest high-value refactoring there is.
mechanism: Heuristics: same-type adjacent params, repeated validation patterns, primitive-typed domain fields. Introduce value objects; move validation into constructors. Tests: the validation tests collapse into one place.
algo: O(signatures) heuristics. The fix is small classes with big payoff.
demo:
# stringly-typed: (host, port, user) all str -- one swap = outage
def connect(host, user, password):
    return 'connecting %s as %s' % (host, user)

print(connect('db-1', 'admin', 's3cret'))
print(connect('admin', 'db-1', 's3cret'), '<- swapped args, still "works": PRIMITIVE OBSESSION')
print()
print('fix: Host, User, Password value types -- the compiler catches the swap')
print('money as float, phone as str: validate once in the constructor, not everywhere')

title: Smell dashboards
description: Smell dashboards trend the codebase's health over time: smell counts by category, hotspot maps (smelly + churny files), and the ratchet (are we getting better?). They turn refactoring from heroic episodes into steady practice — the team watches the trend line, not just the alerts. The key metric is not total smells (legacy is grandfathered) but new smells per PR and hotspot movement.
mechanism: Nightly analysis -> time series DB -> dashboards. Hotspot = normalized(smell density) x normalized(churn). Alerts on hotspot growth, not absolute counts.
algo: O(codebase) nightly; trends are the product.
demo:
# hotspot map: smelly AND churny = fix first
files = [
    ('payments.py', 9, 30),  # (smells, commits/month)
    ('util.py', 8, 2),
    ('checkout.py', 5, 25),
    ('config.py', 1, 1),
]
print('%-14s %6s %6s %8s' % ('file', 'smells', 'churn', 'hotspot'))
for f, s, c in sorted(files, key=lambda x: x[1] * x[2], reverse=True):
    print('%-14s %6d %6d %8d %s' % (f, s, c, s * c, '<- hotspot' if s * c > 100 else ''))
print('trend the hotspots; alert on growth, not absolutes')

title: Team workflows for smells
description: Tools find smells; teams fix them — the workflow matters more than the detector. Working patterns: boy-scout rule (leave it cleaner than you found it) for small smells, dedicated refactoring time (10-20% of sprints) for big ones, and the hotspot list as the shared backlog. The anti-pattern is the 'refactoring sprint' that rewrites everything and breaks trust. Steady, visible, boring progress wins.
mechanism: Boy-scout for small; backlog for big; ratchet in CI for new. Review culture: smell findings are suggestions, not accusations. Measure: hotspot trend, not blame.
algo: Organizational, not algorithmic — but it determines whether the tools matter.
demo:
print('WORKFLOW')
print('1. boy-scout: fix small smells in code you already touch (no permission needed)')
print('2. backlog : hotspot list, top item per sprint (10-20% capacity)')
print('3. ratchet : CI fails on NEW smells (grandfather the old)')
print('4. review  : findings are suggestions, not accusations')
print()
print('steady, visible, boring progress beats the heroic rewrite')
